source.title: Does Data Scaling Lead to Visual Compositional Generalization?
source.authors: Arnas Uselis; Andrea Dittadi; S. Oh

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether scaling training data improves visual compositional downstream performance and reports conditions where increasing data quantity provides little or no benefit. It does not test language-model cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports accuracy and representation-structure results, not held-out cross-entropy or fitted power laws. Its measurements of data quantity and visual compositional accuracy bear on V6. Results about increasing concept diversity are recorded as findings not covered by a claim version; citations to language-model scaling laws are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: The paper sets out to test the scaling premise, citing Kaplan and Hoffmann. It varies in-distribution training-set size (7.5k–120k samples) for from-scratch vision classifiers and reports how OOD compositional accuracy responds. It finds limited or no gain, which bears on V6 (performance improving predictably with data scale). It fits no loss curves or power laws, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that more training data alone does not yield compositional generalization and that combinatorial diversity is the key factor, inducing linearly factored representations. They also find pretrained models (CLIP, DINO) beat from-scratch ResNet-50 and show partial linear structure. Those models still generalize reliably only with diverse combinations, so 'pre-training is not a substitute for data diversity.'
record.recipe_differences: Controlled visual classification and compositional OOD accuracy experiments, rather than language-model held-out loss sweeps or scaling-law fits.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with data quantity versus concept diversity and combination exposure; MPI3D shows no benefit from more ID data at n = 3, k = 2.

fits_no_version.finding: Raising the number of concept values (n) or the number of observed combinations (k) at fixed dataset size improves OOD compositional accuracy. Linear, orthogonal representation structure emerges above ~75% coverage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For visual compositional generalization, combinatorial diversity of training data matters more than raw sample count.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025)
record.problems: The study measures visual compositional accuracy rather than loss, and its main controlled experiments focus on two labeled concepts. The 4× quantity result is reported as an aggregate across datasets, without per-dataset numerical values or uncertainty estimates; some appendix results are presented only in figures. The paper also uses oracle model selection on test performance.
record.rows_left_out: No separately stated numeric outcomes for individual dataset-size points were extracted from Figure 4 or Figure 13; the corresponding aggregate or explicit caption-level findings are recorded in r1 and r2. No loss measurements or power-law fits are reported.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss, no parameter/token/compute sweep, no power-law fit.
No compute budget or compute-optimal allocation.
A ViT depth/width sweep exists (App. C.5) but reports OOD accuracy relative to ResNet-50, not loss at fixed parameter count.
Vision models are studied, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.

Data scale spans only ~4–16× at small sizes. No model-size sweep, no predictability from pretraining loss, no language-model downstream tasks. Pretrained-model comparisons (CLIP, DINO) are not controlled scale sweeps.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices examined.

missing.what: ViT trained from scratch on FunnySprites: OOD accuracy 66.0 at 60k samples vs 57.3 at 120k (ViT†). More data gave lower OOD accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: The V6 link is a stretch in scope. These are small synthetic vision classification tasks over a narrow data range, with OOD accuracy as the measure; no scaling curves are fitted. The results are best read as qualifying V6 for compositional OOD generalization rather than testing language-model downstream predictability. Oracle test-set model selection favours the models, which strengthens the negative data-scaling result. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute sweep, or power-law fit.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss.
No compute budget, compute-optimal allocation, or parameter/token scaling.
Architecture comparisons concern visual compositional accuracy, not held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns vision models but does not test whether a power-law loss form holds in vision or other training regimes.
Tests data-quantity scaling for visual compositional OOD accuracy, not performance on other downstream tasks or predictability from pretraining loss.
Does not examine fitted scaling-law exponents, loss-curve bending, or fitting choices.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Increased in-distribution training set size while keeping the compositional setting fixed.

conditions.value: Shapes3D, CMNIST, dSprites, and FSprites; reported across all datasets
7,500, 15,000, and 30,000 samples for Shapes3D and CMNIST; up to 120,000 for dSprites and FSprites; text describes a 4× increase

rows.measure: Accuracy on unseen combinations and the ID–OOD accuracy gap
rows.value: After increasing training data by 4×, accuracy drops of 60–80% on unseen combinations remained across datasets; the text says quantity only helps reduce the gap and does not solve it.
rows.note: Aggregate result across the named datasets; the text does not give separate numeric values for each dataset.
rows.check: Link and state are correct: the gap shrinks somewhat with 4× data but 60–80% drops remain. Note that the 60–80% figure is the authors' aggregate and differs from the 27–95% range in Fig. 3(a), which uses n=3, k=2. Results use oracle checkpoint selection on the test set.
